strengths: Novel problem formulation with explicit emphasis on stroke order for sketch-based 3D generation, validated through ablation studies showing 8% F-score improvement
Valuable multi-category open-source dataset (VRSketch2Shape) combining 20,838 synthetic and 900 real VR sketches with fine-tuning potential
Strong quantitative results: 82% improvement over baselines on new dataset (F-score 56.8 vs 31.1), and effective generalization from synthetic to real sketches
Well-engineered synthetic sketch generation pipeline with thoughtful stages (surface sampling, salience extraction, spline fitting, stroke ordering)
Comprehensive ablation study (Table 3) systematically validating each design choice and demonstrating robustness to partial sketches
Practical demonstration of few-shot adaptation and sketch completion capability, showing utility for interactive design workflows
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing components (BERT + SDFusion) with straightforward adaptations; no novel architectural contributions to shape generation or sequence modeling

Problematic practical limitations for claimed VR use case: inference requires 50+ hours for batch processing and 10+ hours for individual sketches, making interactive design infeasible

Underspecified technical details: conditioning mechanism for SDFusion is not clearly explained; BERT's adaptation for geometric sequences lacks justification; stroke ordering heuristic (depth-first reversal) poorly motivated

Limited generalization analysis: evaluation concentrates on furniture; no zero-shot experiments on unseen categories; no analysis of how performance degrades with geometric complexity
Statistical rigor absent: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs; F-score threshold (δ=0.02) appears arbitrary without justification; no significance testing
Baseline comparison fairness concerns: LAS-Diffusion uses 2D renderings while this method uses native 3D sketches; comparison with Luo et al. lacks quantitative analysis of geometric differences
Simple dataset alignment methodology using bounding box diagonal matching; no analysis of alignment quality or its impact on model training

strengths: Novel problem formulation explicitly modeling temporal/sequential structure of VR sketches, with clear motivation over treating sketches as static data
Valuable open-source dataset contribution (VRSketch2Shape) as first benchmark for sequential VR sketch-to-3D generation with 20,838 synthetic and 900 real pairs
Comprehensive technical pipeline from synthetic sketch generation through real collection with practical surface snapping mechanism to reduce depth ambiguity
Strong empirical results with substantial improvements over baselines (e.g., F-score 64.3 vs 48.8 vs Luo et al.), consistent across metrics
Thorough ablation study (Table 3) demonstrating importance of stroke ordering, augmentation, and pretraining components
Well-designed synthetic sketch generation leveraging heuristic pipeline (surface sampling, salience-based filtering, Bézier spline fitting, depth-first stroke ordering)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components (BERT sequence encoding, SDFusion shape generation) are existing techniques; contribution is primarily application-level rather than algorithmic

Severely limited real sketch data (900 total) with heavy bias toward chairs (~1,005 from one category per text); collected from only 15 participants after brief tutorial, raising quality and diversity concerns
Small test set (400 samples, 100 per category) insufficient for reliable statistical conclusions; no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing provided

Weak baseline evaluation: only two comparisons (LAS-Diffusion, Luo et al.); missing comparisons with recent sketch-to-3D or state-of-the-art 3D generation methods; no attempted adaptation of excluded baselines
Insufficient analysis of domain gap between synthetic and real sketches; limited evidence that synthetic sketches adequately represent human sketching patterns

Critical reproducibility gaps: surface snapping mechanism underspecified (threshold, algorithm), hyperparameter choices (L=10 Fourier bands) unjustified, augmentation strategies appear ad-hoc, VR interface implementation details missing
Presentation issues: inconsistency between 900 and 1,005 real sketches reported in different sections; notation in Section 4.1 unclear; limited articulation of why sequential information is crucial
Dataset scope limited to 4 categories; generalization to other object types unknown; high CD reconstruction values (~2,500) in Fig. 7 suggest modest reconstruction quality
Frozen VQ-VAE encoder may constrain learned representations for sketch-conditioned generation; inference requires 100 DDIM steps with no discussion of latency for interactive use
Missing critical analyses: no failure case examination beyond brief acknowledgment, no sensitivity studies on key hyperparameters, no user study comparing VR sketches to free-hand alternatives

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem addressing the gap in sequential VR sketch-to-3D generation where temporal order is critical
Valuable dataset contribution (VRSketch2Shape) with 20,838 synthetic and 900 real sketch-shape pairs, first open-access multi-category dataset for this task
Thoughtful synthetic data generation pipeline with principled approach to stroke ordering combining spatial proximity and depth-first traversal
Comprehensive experimental validation including ablation studies (Table 3), few-shot adaptation scenarios, and cross-modal shape completion
Solid technical approach using established components (BERT encoder, SDFusion decoder) appropriately adapted for sequential sketch data
Strong qualitative results demonstrating coherent, topologically faithful shape generation from sketches
Explicit commitment to open-source release of code and data enhancing community reproducibility
weaknesses: Mixed and sometimes contradictory quantitative results: F-score improves substantially but Chamfer Distance significantly degrades (26.1→37.0 on 3DVRChair, 26.6→42.2 for all categories vs Luo et al.), contradicting claims of superior geometry accuracy
Limited baseline comparisons with only two baselines not specifically designed for sequential sketches; no comparisons with other recent sketch-based 3D generation or order-aware methods
Real-world evaluation limited to only 900 sketches from 15 trained participants across 4 object categories; no user studies validating whether generated shapes match user intent
Stroke ordering heuristic is oversimplified; 10% stochasticity parameter appears arbitrary without justification, sensitivity analysis, or validation against ground-truth human sketching order
Insufficient analysis of synthetic-to-real domain gap; few-shot adaptation plateaus suggest synthetic data doesn't fully capture real sketching behavior, but root causes aren't investigated
Limited architectural novelty: encoder (modified BERT) and decoder (SDFusion) are existing methods; primary contribution is problem formulation and dataset
Partial sketch completion handling (Section 5.2, Figure 6) under-evaluated with only qualitative comparisons and no quantitative metrics despite being important for practical applications
Computational efficiency not addressed; 50 hours for synthetic generation and 10 hours fine-tuning mentioned casually with no comparison to baselines

strengths: Novel problem formulation explicitly modeling stroke order in VR sketch-to-shape generation, addressing a genuine gap where prior work discards temporal information
Significant empirical improvements: >60% Chamfer distance reduction and >40% F-score improvement over prior work (Luo et al.)
Comprehensive dataset contribution (VRSKETCH2SHAPE) with 20.8k synthetic + 900 hand-drawn sketches across 4 categories, including surface-snapping mechanism for improved data quality
Thorough experimental validation with extensive ablation studies (Table 4), few-shot adaptation analysis (Fig. 5), free-hand sketch evaluation (Table 3), and supplementary materials (A-1 through A-8)
Effective synthetic-to-real generalization: model trained only on synthetic data performs strongly in zero-shot setting, requiring minimal fine-tuning
Strong robustness to partial sketches enabling cross-modal shape completion, with performance remaining high even with 50% of sketch sequence
Clear and well-written presentation with informative figures and comprehensive related work coverage
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: sketch encoder is straightforward BERT adaptation with minor modifications (Fourier features instead of raw coordinates); shape generator directly reuses SDFUSION without significant adaptation

Insufficient mechanistic analysis of why order matters: while ablations show performance drops without order (56.8→48.9 F-score), there is no attention visualization, feature analysis, or principled explanation of what temporal dependencies are learned

Contradictory evidence on order importance: Table A-1[C] shows reversing stroke order has minimal effect (56.2 vs 56.8) while scrambling points causes clear degradation, questioning the centrality of ordering to the narrative

Synthetic sketch generation pipeline lacks validation: heuristic components (salient point extraction, Bézier fitting, DFS ordering with 10% stochasticity) appear ad-hoc without analysis of domain gap or comparison to human sketching patterns

Significant geometric quality limitations: acknowledged 'slightly oversmooth' reconstructions due to frozen VQ-VAE and 64³ resolution constraint; no justification for frozen VQ-VAE or exploration of end-to-end training

Limited generalization to unseen categories: evaluation on out-of-distribution classes (Appendix A-5) reveals model struggles significantly, reconstructing trucks/beds as table-like structures, indicating heavy reliance on learned priors rather than sketch understanding
Inference latency of 6.6 seconds per shape incompatible with interactive design workflows; faster inference via DDIM reduction (Table A-2) comes with diminishing returns
Modest real dataset scale: 900 sketches with category imbalance (300 chairs vs 200 tables/cabinets/airplanes) limits diversity and robustness assessment

Baseline comparison limitations: only two baselines (Luo et al., LAS-Diffusion); cannot evaluate Chen et al. [7] due to unavailable code; dataset improvements may partially explain performance gains, as Luo et al. also substantially improves on proposed dataset
Hyperparameter choices under-justified: augmentation rates (15%/30%/20%), Fourier frequency L=10, transformer depth of 6 lack sensitivity analysis or principled design rationale
Statistical rigor concerns: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing reported; single runs without multiple random seeds; user study with only 38 participants

Surface snapping dependency: main training uses idealized snapped sketches; while robustness to unsnapped inputs shown in A-3, practical applicability may require infrastructure not available to typical users

strengths: Comprehensive dataset contribution: First open-source multi-category VR sketch dataset with 20,838 synthetic + 900 real samples across 4 categories, addressing data scarcity in the field
Strong empirical results: Substantial improvements over baselines (>60% CD reduction, >40% F-score improvement) with thorough ablation studies validating design choices
Solid experimental validation: Multiple evaluation protocols (zero-shot, few-shot, unseen categories), user study, and extensive supplementary analyses
Practical design considerations: Surface-snapping mechanism effectively reduces depth ambiguity; evaluation on free-hand and partial sketches demonstrates robustness
Well-motivated problem: Clear articulation of why unordered point cloud representations discard important information about sketch connectivity and structure
weaknesses: 'Order matters' claim significantly overstated by ablations: Removing stroke ordering drops F-score only 8.6% (56.8→48.9); reversing order has minimal effect (0.6% drop); removing structured representation entirely drops 26 points. Primary benefit is structured vs. unordered representation, not order per se

Limited technical novelty: BERT encoder with Fourier encodings is straightforward adaptation; SDFusion used as-is without modification; essentially combines existing techniques without methodological innovation

Heuristic synthetic sketch generation unvalidated: No empirical validation that synthetic sketches match real sketching behavior; synthetic sketches show unrealistic geometric alignment (CD 5.5 vs. real >13); design choices (curvature threshold 15, max spline degree 2) lack justification

Serious generalization limitations inadequately discussed: Unseen category results (Figure A-5) show clear failures (trucks→tables, beds→chairs), suggesting model learns category-specific priors rather than generalizable mapping; only 4 training categories limits applicability

Synthetic-to-real gap: Large performance drop zero-shot (F-score ~42) vs. fine-tuned (64.3); model primarily trained on synthetic heuristic data; suggests exploitation of synthetic data properties rather than robust sketch-to-shape learning

Limited practical applicability: 6.6 seconds per shape too slow for interactive design; 64³ SDF resolution with acknowledged oversmoothness; no evaluation of usability in actual design workflows; no multi-object or scene support
Incomplete baseline comparisons: Chen et al. [7] unavailable; only one main VR sketch baseline (Luo et al. 2023); recent methods like VRsketch2Gaussian (2025) in references but not compared

Limited dataset scope: Only 4 furniture-like categories; 900 real samples from 15 annotators; no analysis of sketch distribution or statistics (strokes per sketch, complexity metrics); single objects only

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: Compelling argument that temporal stroke ordering encodes design intent; moves beyond treating sketches as unordered point clouds
Substantial dataset contribution: 20,838 synthetic + 900 real sketch-shape pairs with preserved temporal annotation; surface-snapping reduces misalignment significantly (CD: 55.6→5.5)
Strong empirical results: 60% CD reduction and 40% F-score improvement over Luo et al. [42]; robust zero-shot synthetic-to-real transfer; effective on partial sketches

Comprehensive evaluation: Thorough ablations (Table 4), multi-protocol testing (3DVRCHAIR, new dataset, few-shot adaptation, free-hand, unseen categories), user study (38 participants, 1,900 ratings), supplementary analyses
Technical soundness: Clear architectural choices justified; BERT-based sequential encoder is appropriate for ordered data; implementation details support reproducibility
Practical contributions: Open-source dataset will benefit community; addresses real bottleneck (data scarcity) in prior work
weaknesses: Overclaimed core narrative: Title/framing suggest order is critical, but ablation shows reverse order yields only 0.6 F-score drop (56.2 vs 56.8); supplementary material reframes as 'consistent structure matters' rather than specific ordering

Limited technical novelty: Encoder is straightforward BERT adaptation with Fourier features; SDFUSION used off-the-shelf; synthetic generation relies on standard geometric heuristics (sampling→filtering→spline fitting→DFS); primary novelty in problem formulation, not methods

Synthetic sketch generation concerns: Heuristic DFS ordering with random skipping unlikely reflects realistic human drawing; design choices justified by downstream performance (circular reasoning); no validation that synthetic sketches are perceptually/structurally realistic

Dataset scope limitations: Only 4 categories (furniture-heavy: 300 chairs, 200 each others); 15 annotators for real sketches; surface snapping + reference shapes unrepresentative of free-form VR sketching; unseen category evaluation (A-5) reveals concerning prior-driven failures (trucks→tables)

Evaluation weaknesses: Limited baselines (Chen et al. [7] unavailable); modest user study (40 sketches, 100 pairs); Luo et al. also improves substantially when retrained on authors' data, suggesting benchmark/training improvements may drive gains; Chamfer Distance and F-score have known metric limitations

Architectural constraints: 64³ VQ-VAE resolution limits detail (acknowledged 'slightly oversmooth'); inference time (6.61s) impractical for interactive design; no end-to-end training to lift resolution bottleneck

Incomplete analysis: Why reverse order has negligible impact needs deeper investigation; limited failure case analysis; partial sketch experiments lack theoretical grounding; sketcher expertise impact (A-6) underdeveloped
Presentation issues: Important framing revisions relegated to appendix; 'learning-free' pipeline oversells unsupervised nature (requires parameter tuning); dense Figure 3
